As markers, they are said briefly and with a suspended tone, like a pause for thought: «Pues…», «Bueeeno…». In fast speech, “pues” often becomes “pos” or “ps”.

On Monday 9 February, Señor Dan woke up at half past five, although his alarm was set for six. He showered, shaved, put on a clean shirt and sat down at the computer at five to seven, with a cup of coffee he never got round to tasting. Ana had forbidden them to check the website more than once a week, on Mondays, and he had decided that Monday began at exactly seven o’clock. At one second past seven, he clicked.

The page took an eternity to load. Then a table appeared with his name, his candidate number and, in the last column, a single word: APTO. Below it was the mark: seventy-nine. Señor Dan sat staring at the screen without moving. Then he took out of a drawer the table he had made in November, where he had calculated seventy-eight with a margin of error of three points, and wrote next to it, in very small, very neat handwriting: “Within the margin.” Only then did he allow himself to smile.

His wife found him like that, table in hand, and asked whether he had passed. He told her yes, but that wasn’t the important thing. The important thing, he explained, was that his prediction method had worked. His wife, who had known him for thirty-eight years, took the table out of his hands, kissed him and said: “Well, Dan, fine, your method is marvellous. Now call Costel.” Señor Dan obeyed, although first he put the table in a plastic sleeve.

Costel was on the road, near Pitești, with a load of furniture for Sibiu. When he saw Señor Dan’s call on his phone, he pulled into the first petrol station he found, parked any old how across two spaces, and discovered he couldn’t remember his password for the website. He had written it down somewhere. Probably in his vocabulary notebook. Probably in the vocabulary notebook he had left at home. So he did what he always did when something went wrong: he called Ana.

Ana was making Rosa Elena’s breakfast. She put him on speaker, opened her laptop on the kitchen table, between the bread and the jam, and asked Costel to read her his candidate number. Meanwhile, Señor Dan joined the call and announced his mark with an engineer’s calm that fooled nobody. Costel congratulated him at the top of his voice. Rosa Elena, who understood nothing, also congratulated him at the top of her voice, because she liked shouting. Then there was a very long silence while Costel’s page loaded.

Ana asked him whether he was sitting down. Costel replied that he was at a petrol station and, honestly, there was nowhere to sit. Ana took a deep breath and read: pass, seventy-four. In reading comprehension, seventeen out of twenty-five. In written expression, eighteen. In the oral test, sixteen. And in listening comprehension, the part he had feared most, twenty-three out of twenty-five. Costel said nothing for a few seconds. Then he said: “So… both of us?” And then, much louder: “The weather forecast, eh?! I told you so!”

Then he burst into tears, in front of the pumps, with his phone in his hand. The young man working at the petrol station, a student of about twenty, came out worried to ask if something was wrong. Costel explained, through his tears, that he had passed his Spanish exam. The young man stood looking at him, not quite knowing what to say. Then he told him his grandmother also cried at Mexican soap operas, and bought him a coffee. Costel drank it standing by the lorry, and left him a tip bigger than the coffee.

Then he carried on towards Sibiu, with Spanish radio on at full volume. At eleven they gave the weather forecast: snow in the Pyrenees, rain in Galicia, sun in Andalusia. Costel understood it all and repeated it aloud, word for word, like a happy parrot. On a bend near Râmnicu Vâlcea he realised he was singing along to a song on the radio whose words he didn’t know, making them up in Spanish. He thought that a year earlier he wouldn’t even have dared make them up.

When they hung up, Ana opened her notebook at the last page and looked at the two marks she had pencilled in January. Next to Señor Dan’s name she had written seventy-nine. Next to Costel’s, seventy-six. She had been out by two points. She didn’t tell anyone for a long time, because she thought it unprofessional. But that same afternoon, at the Instituto Cervantes, she told a colleague, who told another, and by six o’clock the whole department knew.

Costel called Zoltán from the next petrol station. Zoltán was in Austria, loading crates of beer, and it took him a moment to understand. When he finally did, he started shouting in Hungarian, and then, with the help of his translation app, sent him a message in Spanish: “You pass bigger than Hungary. I proud like lorry.” Costel replied that it still made no sense. Zoltán replied: “Pues eso.” Costel never found out where he had learnt it, but he had to admit it was used perfectly.

His grandson Álex called him from Valencia at lunchtime. He had seen the voice message in the family group and was impressed. “Grandpa, literally, you’re a legend,” he said. “I mean, seventy-four? My friends don’t get that even in Spanish class.” Costel asked him whether you could say “literal” like that, with nothing after it. Álex explained that yes, it was like “seriously”, but more modern. Costel wrote it in his vocabulary notebook, under “flipar” and “renta”, and promised to use it in the C1. Álex begged him not to.

His daughter called him in the afternoon, from the hospital in Valencia where she worked. They spoke in Romanian, as always, but at the end she switched to Spanish without warning, to test him. Costel answered without thinking, in Spanish, for five minutes straight. His daughter fell silent. Then she said: “Well, Dad, now you’ve got no excuse. This summer you come and talk to my in-laws, who have spent ten years thinking you can’t speak.” Costel promised he would go. And that, just in case, he would bring sarmale.

On Thursday they celebrated at Ecaterina’s. Mrs Florica arrived with the pot of sarmale she had won in the bet, although nobody quite understood why the winner had to bring the food. She explained that that was how bets worked in her family: the winner cooked, so the losers wouldn’t be sad. Señor Dan arrived with his table framed, and hung it himself on the wall of Ecaterina’s living room, next to Faustino’s 1985 photo, without asking permission. Ecaterina decided it could stay there for a week.

Rosa Elena had made diplomas for them both, with coloured card, felt-tip pens and lots of glitter. On Costel’s she had drawn a lorry with a crown; on Señor Dan’s, a bridge with a crown. On both she had written, in huge, slightly crooked letters, the word “APTO”, which Ana had taught her to write that very morning. Señor Dan looked at the diploma for a long time and said he would hang it in his living room, next to his engineering degree. His wife said they would see about that.

Ecaterina gave each of them an envelope. Inside was a handwritten card, in Spanish, with a single sentence: “I can’t correct you any more: now you speak like two madrileños who make mistakes with style.” Costel asked her what “with style” meant. Ecaterina answered: “Just that, Costel. When you make mistakes, it sounds like Spanish.” Costel thought about it for a while and said it was the nicest compliment he had ever been paid, after Andrés’s on the calle del Prado, the day he asked whether he was the lorry driver who cried in Hungary.

In Madrid, meanwhile, Andrei was living his last week as an intern, and Begoña still said nothing. Lucas was on the verge of a nervous breakdown. He had prepared a list of arguments for Andrei, in case he had to negotiate, and had made him rehearse them in the bar downstairs. Andrei rehearsed them out of politeness, but without conviction. He told Lucas that if Begoña wanted him to stay, she would tell him, and if she didn’t, no argument would change her mind. Lucas replied: “Well yeah, man, but at least give it a go…”

On Monday the 23rd, at nine sharp, Begoña called him into her office. She asked him to close the door. Lucas, on the other side, pressed his ear to the glass without the slightest shame. Begoña took off her glasses and said: “Right. Let’s see. The internship ends on Friday. So we need to talk.” Andrei nodded. Begoña took a piece of paper out of a drawer. “It’s a one-year contract. It’s not much money. I mean, you won’t get rich. But it’s a contract.” Andrei looked at the paper. Then he looked at her. “Well… OK,” he said. “I mean, yes.”

Begoña asked him whether he didn’t want to read it before signing. Andrei replied that she had taught him to understand a photo before taking it, and he had understood that contract months ago, even though nobody had shown it to him. Begoña looked at him for a moment with something like a smile. Then she said: “Don’t get poetic, Lucas is listening.” On the other side of the glass, Lucas jumped, banged his head on the shelf and shouted “¡olé!” at the top of his lungs. The whole agency heard the news before Andrei’s mother did.

Andrei called his parents at lunchtime. His mother burst into tears at once. His father was silent, then said: “Right. Well, very good.” And straight away he asked three technical questions about the contract: the exact duration, the probation period and whether it included health insurance. Andrei didn’t know the answer to any of them. His father told him to read it carefully, that a contract was like a bridge, you had to look underneath it. Then, as they were about to hang up, he added more quietly: “I’m proud of you, you know.”

Marta found out in the evening, when Andrei came home with a bottle of cava and a bag of churros. She asked whether that meant he was staying in the room off the hallway. Andrei said yes, if she didn’t mind. Marta replied: “Well, of course. Who else is going to make the coffee in the mornings?” Then she turned serious and told him her grandfather would have been pleased: he always said a house with a photographer in it never ran out of memories. They drank a toast in the hallway, in front of the green sign.

The next day, the news reached Seville and the Cuesta de Moyano. Pilar sent Andrei a very short message: “My father always said that good photographers, like good booksellers, stay.” Faustino, who had no mobile phone, sent his congratulations via Lola, on one condition: that the first portrait Andrei took under contract should be of him, in his red beret, so he could hang it in his stall next to the five-hundred-peseta note. Andrei agreed. Faustino also demanded that it be flattering.

Ecaterina, for her part, had finished correcting the proofs on 13 February. She had found forty-one typos, three wrong dates and a comma in the wrong place, on page 98. She sent them back to Barcelona by express post, with a note for Inés: “Well, that’s it. Please don’t send them to me again, because if I read them again, I’ll change them again.” Inés replied that the book would go to the printer on 1 April and would go on sale on the 23rd, World Book Day.

23 April. Ecaterina repeated it aloud, and thought it a very fitting date, because it was the day Cervantes and Shakespeare died, and the day when people in Barcelona give each other books and roses. Inés wanted to launch it first in Madrid, at El Mostrador, on the 23rd itself, and then in Seville, on the 25th, at the bookshop in Triana that Pilar had chosen. When Lola found out, she spent a whole afternoon measuring the café with a tape measure to work out how many chairs would fit. Faustino offered to bring the ones from his stall.

Meanwhile, at Rosa Elena’s kindergarten, the teacher had finally agreed to the Friday Spanish class, on one condition: that she, the teacher, would teach it, and Rosa Elena would only be her “assistant”. Rosa Elena agreed, but on the first Friday she took control of the class within five minutes. She taught her classmates “hola”, “olé”, “por fin” and “es que”. That last one was a mistake. Since then, every time a child arrived late, lost a glove or hit another child, they began the sentence with “es que…”, and the teacher didn’t know whether to laugh or cry.

Things were happening at El Mostrador too. One February afternoon, a customer returned a borrowed book of poems and Lola found a handwritten note inside: “To the translator who came back: thank you for reminding us that letters must be sent.” It wasn’t signed. Lola photographed it and sent it to Ecaterina, who read it three times. Then Lola stuck it in the customers’ notebook, on the first page. From then on, every week a new note addressed to the translator turned up, even though the book hadn’t come out yet.

Ecaterina, meanwhile, went on translating the book into Romanian in the mornings. The Bucharest publisher that had published “Librăria de pe strada Huertas” wanted the Romanian version for the autumn. The hard part wasn’t the words but the markers, as Ana called them: those “pues”, “o sea” and “hombre” that sounded so natural in Andrés’s mouth in the original and became something else in Romanian. Ecaterina said that translating one of Andrés’s “pues” was harder than translating a Machado poem, because a poem has rules, and a “pues” only has a voice.

On Friday the 27th, the last day of the internship, Andrei arrived at the agency at eight. There was an envelope on his desk. Inside there was no note, just a key: the agency key, the one staff photographers had so they could get in at night when there was a story. Begoña, from her office, without looking up, said: “Right, well. Welcome. I mean, again.” Lucas organised a lunch at the bar downstairs to celebrate. Begoña didn’t go, but she paid the bill.

That same night, late, Ecaterina called Marta. She told her about the passes, the contract, the typos. Marta told her that Andrei had fallen asleep on the sofa with the agency key in his hand, like a child with a new toy. They both laughed. Then Ecaterina was quiet for a moment and asked what her grandfather would have said about all this. Marta didn’t hesitate. She said he would have pretended not to be impressed, switched on the lamp and said only: “Pues muy bien.” And that with that he would have said everything.

That night, the club’s group chat was on fire. Andrei sent a photo of the key on top of the green sign. Ecaterina sent a photo of the corrected proofs, with the red pencil on top. Señor Dan sent, once again, his framed table. Rosa Elena sent, with Ana’s help, a ten-second voice message in which she shouted “¡es que olé!”, which nobody understood. Finally, at midnight, Costel summed up the month in a single message, from a car park near Sibiu: “So there you go: two passes, a contract and a book in April. I mean, February hasn’t been bad at all.”
